quickAnswer: Fuel oil heats 49.0% of Carlisle homes and electricity only 5.3%, which ranks 48th of the 50 towns (ACS 2022). With 93.4% of homes detached houses, the typical system to size here is one house with its own oil, gas or propane plant.
body: ## Detached houses almost everywhere

Carlisle counts 1,875 housing units, and 1,751 of them are single-family detached houses. That is 93.4% according to the Census Bureau's 2022 American Community Survey (ACS 2022), the 2nd-highest share among the 50 towns Mass HVAC serves, while the middle town sits at 76.7%. Townhouses add 31 units and buildings of five or more units add 64. Together, every multi-unit building holds 93 units, or 5.0%.

Renting is unusual: 108 of 1,787 occupied homes (6.0%), 47th of 50. Another 88 units, 4.7%, stand vacant, which ranks 19th and sits above the 3.6% of the middle town. For anyone planning equipment, the main picture is a stand-alone house with its own heating plant rather than a shared boiler serving many apartments.
## Oil at the top, electric heat near the bottom

Fuel oil or kerosene heats 876 occupied homes, 49.0%, putting Carlisle 18th of 50 and far above the 36.5% of the middle town. Utility gas follows with 614 homes (34.4%), 31st. Electricity heats 95 homes (5.3%), the 48th-highest share.

With nearly half the town on oil, a worn-out boiler often leads to the same three-way comparison: a new oil unit, gas if a main passes the house, or a heat pump. Where no main runs, gas is simply not on the list. A heat pump adds electrical load, and a house that has little electric equipment might need its panel looked at. That is general knowledge, not a survey of local panels.
## Mostly built from 1960 to 1999

The median Carlisle home was built in 1977, against 1975 for the middle town. Two bands hold most of the housing: 737 units (39.3%) from 1960 to 1979 and 692 (36.9%) from 1980 to 1999. Only 133 units (7.1%) are from 1939 or earlier, which ranks 46th, and 147 (7.8%) are from 2000 or later.

Insulation, windows and air sealing can differ a lot between those decades. We assess the home's heating load before quoting a system, so the new equipment is matched to the house and not to the size of whatever sat in the basement before.
## Land that once belonged to its neighbors

English colonists first settled the area in 1651, on parcels that belonged to the neighboring towns of Acton, Billerica, Chelmsford and Concord. Carlisle became a district of Concord in 1780 and was incorporated as a town by an act of the legislature in 1805. Its name comes from Carlisle, England, the hometown of one of the earliest settlers, James Adams.

Today the town covers 15.5 square miles, with 15.4 of them land and 0.2 water. It lies about 19 miles northwest of Boston and 8 miles south-southwest of Lowell, and it borders Concord, Acton, Westford, Chelmsford, Billerica and Bedford. Conservation land makes up about a quarter of the town's area, including Great Brook Farm State Park and a portion of the Great Meadows National Wildlife Refuge beside the Concord River.
## Which utility handles your rebate

No electric utility is named for Carlisle in our data, and rebates for a heat pump run through whichever one serves your address. Find it on your electric bill before you plan a budget, because the rules differ from one utility to the next, and remember that program terms can change. The 2026 details are on our [heat pump page](/cities/carlisle/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).

faq.q: How common is oil heat in Carlisle?
faq.a: Very common. The 2022 survey counts 876 oil or kerosene homes among the town's occupied homes, 49.0%, which is 18th among the 50 towns. Utility gas is second at 34.4%. If your house burns oil, replacement usually starts with a choice between another oil unit, gas where a main exists, and a heat pump.

faq.a: Not from this page. Rebates run through whichever electric utility serves your address, and that is a fact about your bill, so look there first. Once you know it, masssave.com lists the current terms, which can change. Our heat pump page for Carlisle explains how the 2026 rebate fits the town's housing.

faq.q: Does the age of a Carlisle house change the system size?
faq.a: It can. The town's median home dates from 1977, and most units fall between 1960 and 1999, a span in which insulation and windows can vary. A boiler or furnace sized for the old equipment may be too big or too small now, so a heating load assessment before quoting is the better starting point.

Yes. Owners hold 1,679 of 1,787 households (94.0%), and only 108 households rent. That is the 47th-highest renter share of the 50 towns. In practical terms, the typical equipment project here is a single detached house rather than a building with several households sharing one system.

heating-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Beyond oil, Carlisle splits three ways: utility gas in 614 homes (34.4%), bottled gas in 112 (6.3%, 14th of 50) and wood in 56 (3.1%). A failed boiler or furnace can raise a fuel question as well as a repair question.
body: ## A fuel question inside every replacement

Setting oil aside, the 2022 American Community Survey (ACS 2022) shows Carlisle heating spread over several fuels. Utility gas serves 614 homes (34.4%), 31st of 50. Bottled or tank gas serves 112 homes (6.3%), the 14th-highest share. Wood heats 56 homes (3.1%), and 34 occupied homes report using no heating fuel at all.

With a spread like that, a boiler that dies in January can send an owner in several directions: the same fuel again, a different fuel, or a heat pump. Our [maintenance page](/cities/carlisle/hvac-maintenance-tune-ups) covers keeping whichever system you choose in good shape.
### Gas only where a main passes

Utility gas depends on a main reaching the house, and whether one runs down a given road is a question for the gas company. If a switch is possible, expect a permit. A new gas furnace or boiler normally needs one, plus a final inspection, and only licensed plumbers and gas fitters may pull gas permits in Massachusetts. The town's building department can say what else applies locally.
### Tank fuels and their tanks

Propane and oil both arrive by truck and live in a tank, so a replacement can be a natural time to ask about the tank's age and where it sits. A house without a gas main may end up comparing those two fuels against a heat pump.
### Older houses, honest sizing

Carlisle has 1,036 units built before 1980 (55.3%), 32nd of 50, against 57.2% for the middle town. That group includes the 166 units from 1940 to 1959 (8.9%) and the 133 from 1939 or earlier. Insulation work done over the decades can change how much heat a house loses, so a boiler matched to the old nameplate is a guess. We assess the home's heating load before quoting a system, and that number sets the size.
### When the heat stops
Call (508) 786-8755 at any hour, since emergency calls are taken around the clock. Free written estimates come before work starts, and Mass HVAC is licensed and insured.

faq.q: Is gas an option for a Carlisle house that burns oil?
faq.a: Only if a gas main reaches the street or can be extended to it, which the gas company decides. Utility gas heats 34.4% of Carlisle homes today, so the network reaches parts of town. Without a main, the realistic paths are a new oil system, propane or a heat pump.

faq.q: What changes when a house uses bottled gas?
faq.a: Bottled or tank gas is delivered like oil, so the tank, its location and the delivery arrangement are part of the replacement decision. Carlisle ranks 14th of 50 for this fuel, at 112 homes. A heat pump removes the delivery question for the share of the load it carries.

faq.q: How can I tell if a new boiler is the right size?
faq.a: Ask what the size is based on. A match to the old nameplate repeats whatever mistake was made before. A heating load assessment looks at the house itself: its insulation, windows and air leakage. The result tells you the capacity needed, and it can differ from what the old unit offered.

air-conditioning-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Carlisle's owner-occupied homes have a median value of $940,300, 7th of 50, and only 93 units sit in multi-unit buildings. Cooling here is mostly a matter of detached houses, with central, ductless or mixed layouts.
body: ## Cooling detached houses

The 2022 American Community Survey (ACS 2022) puts the median value of an owner-occupied Carlisle home at $940,300. That is 7th-highest of the 50 towns and well above the $579,150 of the middle town. The same survey counts 31 townhouse units (1.7%), 9 units in two-unit buildings, 20 in buildings of three or four units (1.1%) and 64 in buildings of five or more (3.4%).

The numbers point to one kind of project: air conditioning for a single detached house, where the outdoor unit can stand beside the building rather than on a shared wall or balcony. The 93 multi-unit homes make up 5.0% of the housing and rank 46th, so they are the exception.
### Central, ductless or a mix

Central air works when the ducts are in good condition and sized for cooling airflow. Ducts built for heating alone are often too small for it, so a check is sensible. Ductless mini-splits need only a small opening for the line set and serve rooms one at a time. A common answer for a house with one stubborn room is central air for most of it and a ductless head for the rest.
### Electricity in a town that heats with fuel

Electricity heats 95 Carlisle homes (5.3%), 48th of 50, so electric equipment is the exception for winter. Summer cooling is electric by nature. A new central system or several mini-splits can add load to a panel, and an electrician can say whether the panel has room. A heat pump can cool in summer and heat in winter, which may let one system cover both jobs.
### Newer construction

Carlisle has 113 units built since 2010 (6.0%), ranking 35th of 50. Newer houses tend to be tighter, and a tight house is easier to cool with a modest system, as long as it is not oversized. An oversized unit cools fast, shuts off before it dries the air and leaves a damp feel. Matching size to the house avoids that.
### Repair or replace

A failed capacitor, a dirty coil or a slow refrigerant leak is often a repair. A failed compressor on old equipment usually points to replacement. Either way, a free written estimate comes before work starts. For rebates on cooling-capable equipment, see the [heat pump page](/cities/carlisle/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).

faq.q: Can a Carlisle house without ducts still get air conditioning?
faq.a: Yes. A ductless mini-split cools without ductwork, with one indoor head for each area. Detached houses make up 93.4% of the housing here, so a free-standing building with exterior walls is the usual case. How many heads you need depends on the layout and how many rooms you want cooled.

faq.q: Will cooling equipment need electrical work?
faq.a: Sometimes. A central system or several mini-splits draw power, and whether an older panel has room is a question for an electrician or the installer. Settling it before the estimate is signed keeps electrical work from becoming a surprise line later. A single ductless head is often a smaller load than a ducted system.

faq.q: Is it better to repair or replace an old air conditioner?
faq.a: A small part such as a capacitor or a fan motor is usually worth repairing. A failed compressor, a leaking coil or repeated refrigerant top-ups on equipment that has been running for many years usually favors replacement. The written estimate should show both options side by side before you decide.

heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits.quickAnswer: Whole-home Mass Save heat pump rebates need the house weatherized first, and only 147 Carlisle units (7.8%) date from 2000 or later. Which rebate you get depends on the electric utility serving your address.
body: ## What the housing numbers mean for rebates

Mass Save's 2026 whole-home rebate is $2,650 per ton, up to $8,500 per home, and the home must be sufficiently weatherized first. The full terms are on our [statewide heat pump page](/services/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).

The weatherization test is easy to pass for a house built in 2000 or later. In Carlisle, 147 units (7.8%) are that new. The two biggest age bands, 737 units from 1960 to 1979 and 692 from 1980 to 1999, both fall before the cutoff. For those houses, the other routes matter: an assessment that recommends under $1,000 of work, or recommendations from 2013 or later that were completed.
### The utility comes first

The electric utility serving each Carlisle address is not confirmed here, so the rebate path depends on yours. Look at the electric bill, and then read the program terms for that utility before budgeting.
### Oil and propane homes

The fuel mix is why heat pumps get attention here. Oil heats 876 Carlisle homes, bottled gas heats 112, and electricity heats only 95. For the oil and propane group, a heat pump swaps a delivered fuel for electricity over part or all of the year. Utility gas serves 614 homes, so a gas household compares a heat pump against a fuel that arrives through a pipe.
### Whole house or partial

A whole-house system replaces the old plant. A partial setup keeps the boiler or furnace for the coldest hours and lets the heat pump carry the rest of the year, which suits an owner who wants to keep a working oil boiler. Partial-home rebates exist too, and they are smaller per ton.
### Ducted, ductless, or both

A ducted unit can reuse good ductwork. Ductless heads suit a room or two that the main system reaches poorly. In a town where 93.4% of homes are detached houses, either layout normally has an outer wall available for the outdoor unit and line set, although the final placement depends on the house.
### Sizing

A heat pump too small leans on backup heat, and one too large cycles on and off. We assess the home's heating load before quoting a system and show the options in a free written estimate. See also the [cooling page](/cities/carlisle/air-conditioning-installation-repair) for how ductless heads cool single rooms.

faq.q: Do older Carlisle houses qualify for the whole-home rebate?
faq.a: They can, but the weatherization test comes first. Most Carlisle housing was built between 1960 and 1999, before the 2000 cutoff, so the usual route is a Home Energy Assessment. If it recommends less than $1,000 of work, or past recommendations were completed, the home can pass. Terms can change, so confirm them at masssave.com.

faq.q: Can a heat pump work alongside my oil boiler?
faq.a: Yes. A house on oil may have a working boiler its owner prefers to keep. A partial-home setup lets the heat pump carry the mild months and the boiler handle the coldest days. Partial-home rebates are available, and your utility decides which program applies.

faq.q: What if my electric utility is not a Mass Save sponsor?
faq.a: Then the rebate path changes. Some towns have a municipal electric utility with its own heat pump program, and in those places Mass Save rebates generally apply only to homes heated with sponsor-supplied natural gas. Because Carlisle's utility is not confirmed here, check the one on your bill before planning the budget.

hvac-maintenance-tune-ups.quickAnswer: With oil in 876 Carlisle homes (49.0%) and gas in 614, most systems here burn something, and burners need regular attention. Only 6.0% of households rent, so the person scheduling a tune-up is usually the one who owns the house.
body: ## Burners that need attention

The oil number sets the schedule. Oil heats 876 Carlisle homes, and gas heats another 614. Both fuels run a flame, and a flame means soot, combustion settings, vents and safety controls. Oil equipment needs a cleaning every year, and gas equipment benefits from a burner, venting and controls check on a regular basis.
### Owners and renters

The 2022 American Community Survey (ACS 2022) counts 1,679 owner-occupied households (94.0%) and only 108 renters. For an owner there is no landlord between the house and the boiler, so a service visit starts when the owner books it. A tune-up booked on purpose is usually calmer than an emergency call at midnight in a cold snap.
### A calendar for a town of fuel burners
- **Late summer to early fall:** heating tune-ups, before the nights turn cold.
- **Spring:** cooling checks for central air and ductless heads, before the first hot week.
- **After a long absence:** vacancy is 4.7% here, 19th of 50, and a house left empty for months deserves a look before the heat is turned up.
- **Any time:** a new noise, a smell, short cycling or a rising bill is worth a call.
### Age and wear

Equipment that has run for many years wears in predictable places, such as igniters, nozzles, belts and motors. Replacing a worn part during a planned visit is usually cheaper than losing the whole system on a holiday weekend. The 1960 to 1979 and 1980 to 1999 bands hold most of the housing here, so plenty of houses are old enough for this to matter.
### What to have ready

When you call, give the fuel, the approximate age of the system, the make and model on its nameplate, and whatever you have noticed. That shortens the first conversation and helps the technician bring the right parts. Our [heating page](/cities/carlisle/heating-installation-repair) explains what happens when a unit is beyond repair.

faq.q: How often should an oil burner in Carlisle be serviced?
faq.a: Once a year is the usual rule, ideally before the heating season starts. Skipping it lets soot accumulate, which can cut efficiency and lead to a breakdown in the coldest weeks. Since 49.0% of Carlisle homes burn oil, an annual cleaning applies to close to half the town.

faq.q: Do gas systems need a yearly visit too?
faq.a: A yearly visit is a sensible habit. A technician looks at the burner, venting and controls, and checks that combustion is clean and safe. Gas heats 34.4% of Carlisle homes, and those systems tend to run quietly enough that problems can go unnoticed until a cold night.

faq.q: Should I service air conditioning separately?
faq.a: Cooling equipment has its own parts: coils, a condensate drain, electrical connections and refrigerant charge. A spring check, before the first hot week, can catch a problem while it is still a small repair. A heat pump covers both seasons, so its check can be timed for either one.

indoor-air-quality.quickAnswer: Carlisle houses mostly date from 1960 to 1999, with 147 units from 2000 or later and 133 from 1939 or earlier. Leakier and tighter houses have different air problems, and the age bands hint at which ones to suspect.
body: ## Air in houses of different ages

According to the 2022 American Community Survey (ACS 2022), Carlisle's housing splits into familiar bands: 133 units from 1939 or earlier (7.1%), 166 from 1940 to 1959 (8.9%), 737 from 1960 to 1979 (39.3%), 692 from 1980 to 1999 (36.9%) and 147 from 2000 or later (7.8%). Those bands matter because air quality problems often follow construction style.
### Leaky versus tight

Older houses often leak air through gaps, which dilutes some pollutants and also brings in dust, pollen and basement air. Newer houses are usually tighter. That saves energy, and it also keeps moisture, cooking fumes and chemicals from furnishings indoors unless ventilation does its job. The 1960 to 1999 houses sit between those cases, and the answer depends on what has been done to them since.
### Oil, wood and combustion

The survey lists oil in 876 homes, gas in 614 and wood in 56. Any flame appliance should be vented correctly and kept in tune, because combustion byproducts such as carbon monoxide are an air quality issue as well as a safety one. Detectors for carbon monoxide are worth having wherever fuel is burned.
### Humidity

Winter heating can leave indoor air dry, and summer can bring humidity back. Measuring first shows which season is the problem. A humidifier or dehumidifier tied to the system, or a ventilator in a tight house, is a response to a measurement and not a default.
### Ducts and filters

Filters catch what passes through the system, so a clean one of the right grade helps. Duct cleaning makes sense in specific cases, such as visible dirt, mold, or damage from pests or renovation. Where ducts are leaky, sealing them can matter more than cleaning them.
### Testing

Air testing can point to a problem such as high humidity, carbon monoxide or particles, but it is a snapshot of one day. Fixing the source, whether a damp basement, a leaking duct or an unvented appliance, keeps the problem from returning. For equipment upkeep that protects air quality, see the [maintenance page](/cities/carlisle/hvac-maintenance-tune-ups).

faq.q: Do older Carlisle houses have worse air quality?
faq.a: Not automatically. Houses from 1939 or earlier, only 133 units here, often leak more air, which dilutes some pollutants and admits others such as dust and damp air. Tighter houses hold moisture and fumes. The right fix depends on measurements and on the condition of the house, not on its age alone.

faq.q: Is a ventilator worth considering in a tighter house?
faq.a: It can be. If a house is airtight, moisture, cooking fumes and chemicals can build up. A ventilator brings in outdoor air while moving the indoor air out, often passing heat between the two streams. Only 147 Carlisle units date from 2000 or later, so the newest, tightest construction is a small slice of the housing.

faq.q: When does duct cleaning make sense?
faq.a: When ducts are visibly dirty, have mold, or were damaged by pests or a renovation. Without those signs, the money is usually better spent on filters, sealing leaks or controlling humidity. Look at the system first and clean only if there is a reason, then fix the cause so the dirt does not return.
